text.en: Imagine travelling by road from Chhota Nagpur in Jharkhand to Prayagraj in Uttar Pradesh and on to Almora in Uttarakhand. In a few hundred kilometres you would pass a plateau, a plain and then mountains. The surface of the Earth is full of such shapes, called landforms, and each one shapes how people live, work and even worship.

A landform is a physical feature on the surface of the Earth. Landforms take shape over millions of years and are closely linked with the environment and life. They are broadly divided into three categories: mountains, plateaus and plains. Each has its own climate and its own plants and animals. Humans have adapted to all landforms, but the number of people living on each differs a lot from place to place.
Mountains are landforms much higher than the land around them. You can recognise a mountain by its broad base, steep slopes and narrow summit. Height above sea level is called altitude. At high altitude snow may never melt, so the mountain stays permanently snow-capped. At lower altitudes the snow melts every summer and feeds rivers. Other highlands with lower height, gentler slopes and rounded tops are called hills. Most mountains lie in ranges, such as the Himalayas in Asia, the Alps in Europe and the Andes in South America. Some ranges stretch for thousands of kilometres. Mount Everest, between Tibet and Nepal, and Kanchenjunga, between Nepal and Sikkim, are the two highest peaks of the Himalayas. Aconcagua is the highest peak of the Andes in South America. Kilimanjaro in eastern Africa is an isolated mountain that belongs to no range. Mont Blanc is the highest peak of the Alps, and Anamudi in Kerala, also called Anai Peak, is the highest mountain in south India. Tall and sharp mountains like the Himalayas are young in the history of the Earth, though they formed millions of years ago, and they are still growing. Shorter, rounded ranges like the Aravalli are much older and have been worn down by erosion. Mountain slopes often carry montane forest, with conifers such as pine, fir, spruce and deodar, which grow tall and cone shaped with thin pointed leaves. Higher up, the trees give way to grasses, mosses and lichen. Mountain animals include the golden eagle, peregrine falcon, snow leopard, ibex, Himalayan tahr, mountain hare, yak, grey fox and black bear. The Ganga, about 2500 km long, is the largest river that begins in the Himalayas. The Yamuna and the Ghaghara are among its tributaries from the Himalayas, while the Son rises in the Vindhya Range to the south.
Mountain terrain is rough with steep slopes, so regular farming is possible only in some valleys. Farmers cut steps into the slope and grow crops on them, which is called terrace farming. In many mountain regions herding is preferred to farming. Tourism is an important source of income because of the crisp air and scenery. Some tourists come for skiing, hiking, mountaineering and paragliding, and pilgrims have travelled to holy sites for centuries. Too many visitors, however, can harm the fragile mountain environment. Life in the mountains also brings dangers: landslides, avalanches, cloudbursts and flash floods, as well as uncontrolled tourism and heavy snowfall and cold. Bachendri Pal was the first Indian woman to climb Mount Everest, in 1984. Arunima Sinha lost a leg at 22, climbed Everest in 2013 and went on to climb the highest peak of every continent. Many communities treat mountains as sacred. Tibetans call Everest Chomolungma, the Mother Goddess of the World, and Nepalis call it Sagarmatha, the Goddess of the Sky. It is 8848 metres high, the highest mountain in the world. Mount Kailash is sacred to Hindus, Buddhists, Jains and followers of Bon.
A plateau rises above the land around it and has a more or less flat top, with some steep sides. Plateaus can be young or old, and their height varies from a few hundred metres to several thousand. The Tibetan Plateau is the largest and highest in the world, with an average height of 4500 metres, which earned it the name Roof of the World. The Deccan Plateau in central and south India is one of the oldest plateaus and was formed by volcanic activity millions of years ago. Plateaus are called storehouses of minerals, so mining is a major activity. East Africa is famous for gold and diamonds, and the Chhota Nagpur Plateau in India has huge reserves of iron, coal and manganese. Many plateaus have rocky soil, which is less fertile than the soil of plains, so farming is harder. Lava plateaus are an exception because they often have rich black soil. Plateaus are home to spectacular waterfalls such as Victoria Falls on the Zambezi, Hundru Falls on the Subarnarekha, Jog Falls on the Sharavati and Nohkalikai Falls, which drop 340 metres from the Cherrapunji Plateau in Meghalaya.
Plains are landforms with an extensive flat or gently rolling surface and no large hills or deep valleys. They are generally not more than 300 metres above sea level. Floodplains form when rivers from the mountains carry rock, sand and silt, called sediments, and deposit them on the plains. This makes the soil very fertile, so plains are ideal for growing many crops. The first civilisations grew up around rivers in fertile plains, and a large part of the world population still lives on plains. About 40 crore people, more than one-fourth of India, live in the Ganga plain. People fish in the rivers and farm rice, wheat, maize, barley and millets, and fibre crops such as cotton, jute and hemp. Farming used to depend on rain. Now canals and groundwater pumping are used. Irrigation raised production but also reduced groundwater. High population and pollution are other problems of the Ganga plain. Plains have gentle slopes, so rivers are easy to sail and boats carry goods and people. Communities consider a river source and a confluence, where rivers meet, to be sacred and hold festivals there.
Experts name other landforms too. A desert is a large dry expanse with very little precipitation and its own special plants and animals. Some deserts are hot, like the Sahara in Africa and the Thar in the northwest of the Indian Subcontinent. Others are cold, like the Gobi in Asia. People have adapted to most deserts. Communities in the Thar have rich folk songs and legends that grew out of the desert way of life.

problem.en: Which landform? A region has a flat top, steep sides, rich iron and coal, and is 700 metres high.

text.en: Check the shape.

why.en: A flat top with steep sides points to a plateau, not a mountain which has a narrow summit.

text.en: Check the resources.

why.en: Iron and coal are minerals, and plateaus are storehouses of minerals.

text.en: Check the height.

why.en: Plateaus range from a few hundred to several thousand metres, so 700 m fits.

text.en: Name it.

why.en: It is a plateau, like Chhota Nagpur.

prompt.en: Compare mountains, plateaus and plains and say how people live on each.

requiredIdeas.en: Mountains have broad bases, steep slopes and narrow summits and people practise terrace farming, herding and tourism
Plateaus have flat tops, are rich in minerals and support mining
Plains are flat, have fertile floodplain soil and support farming, rivers and cities
Each landform also brings problems, such as landslides, poor soil or water shortage

commonMisconceptions.en: Thinking all plateaus have fertile soil
Thinking plains are always above 300 metres
Thinking mountains are not growing any more

points.en: Landforms are physical features of the Earth: mountains, plateaus and plains, with deserts as another landform.
Mountains have broad bases, steep slopes and narrow summits. Hills are lower with rounded tops.
Plateaus are flat-topped highlands rich in minerals, such as the Deccan and Tibetan Plateaus.
Plains are flat and fertile and have supported civilisations, farming and river transport.
Each landform has opportunities and challenges, and rivers and mountains hold cultural value.
